label.reasoning: The item primarily assesses velocity and displacement under constant acceleration. It also explicitly requires Newton’s second law to explain why a constant net force maintains constant acceleration, so both kinematics and translational dynamics are required.

The item primarily assesses velocity and displacement under constant acceleration. It also explicitly requires Newton’s second law to explain the constant net force associated with constant acceleration, so both kinematics and translational dynamics are required.

The item centers on rolling without slipping and the relationship between translational and rotational motion. Deriving and scaling the bottom speed requires gravitational potential energy, translational and rotational kinetic energy, and conservation of mechanical energy with no dissipative losses.

The item centers on a perfectly inelastic collision, testing momentum conservation experimentally and explaining why kinetic energy is not conserved. It requires linear momentum, impulse, collision concepts, and translational kinetic energy.

The item centers on a perfectly inelastic collision and an experimental test of momentum conservation. It requires linear momentum and impulse concepts from Unit 4, plus kinetic energy and its nonconservation during sticking collisions from Unit 3.

The question centers on rolling without slipping, combining conservation of mechanical energy, translational and rotational kinetic energy, rotational inertia, and the linear–angular speed relation to analyze how bottom speed depends on drop height.

The item centers on buoyancy and Archimedes’ principle applied to a submerged block. Drawing a free-body diagram and expressing equilibrium with gravity, tension, and buoyancy also require forces and Newton’s second law from Unit 2.

The item focuses on orbital speed and period for satellites. It requires Newton’s second law, universal gravitation, and circular-motion dynamics from Unit 2, together with satellite orbital relationships from Unit 6.

The item focuses on orbital speed and period for satellites. It requires Newton’s second law, universal gravitation, and circular-motion dynamics from Unit 2, applied to orbiting satellites in Unit 6.
The item emphasizes how oscillator energy depends on amplitude, using elastic potential energy. It also requires SHM relationships connecting angular frequency, amplitude, and maximum speed.

The item emphasizes how an oscillator’s total mechanical energy depends on amplitude, using spring potential energy. It also requires SHM relationships connecting amplitude, angular frequency, and maximum speed.
The item applies Archimedes’ principle and buoyant force to a submerged block, together with free-body diagrams and Newton’s second law in equilibrium to determine the direction of string tension.

The item centers on relative velocity between the boat, water, and shore. Vector addition and two-dimensional kinematics determine the shore-relative motion, crossing time, and downstream displacement; all required content belongs to Unit 1.

The item assesses experimental measurements and graphical representations of motion used to determine whether acceleration is constant. It requires kinematics, not analysis of the forces causing the cart’s motion.

The item assesses experimental measurement and graphical representation of motion to determine whether acceleration is constant. It requires interpreting position or velocity data over time, without analyzing forces or energy.

The item centers on adding velocities in different reference frames to determine motion relative to shore. Vector components and constant-velocity kinematics are also needed for crossing time and downstream displacement, all within Unit 1.

The question requires a free-body diagram and Newton’s second law to relate the passenger’s upward acceleration to the normal force measured by the scale and distinguish that force from gravitational weight.

The item requires a free-body diagram and Newton’s second law to relate the passenger’s upward acceleration to the normal force measured by the scale and distinguish apparent weight from gravitational weight.

The procedure and derivation center on limiting static friction as an incline reaches the critical angle. Force components, the normal force, and translational equilibrium are needed, all within Unit 2.

The item centers on determining static friction at the threshold of slipping on an incline. Its procedure and derivation require force diagrams, components of gravitational force, normal force, and force balance, all within Unit 2.
The item focuses on circular motion on a frictionless banked curve, requiring a free-body diagram and Newton’s second law applied to vertical equilibrium and radial centripetal acceleration.

The item focuses on circular motion on a frictionless banked curve, requiring a free-body diagram and Newton’s second law to relate normal-force components to centripetal acceleration and vertical equilibrium.

The item centers on conservation of linear momentum during separation. It also requires center-of-mass motion and the distinction between internal and external forces to justify the system’s behavior and compare the carts’ momentum and velocity changes.

The item assesses conservation of linear momentum during an internal interaction, including center-of-mass motion and comparisons of individual momentum and velocity changes. It requires systems and center-of-mass concepts from Unit 2 and momentum concepts from Unit 4.

The central task is determining work from a force-versus-position graph. The remaining parts use the work–energy theorem to determine speed and compare average with instantaneous power, all within Unit 3.
The central task is determining work from a force-versus-position graph. The remaining parts apply the work–energy theorem and distinguish average from instantaneous power, all within Unit 3.

Final-speed comparison centers on conservation of mechanical energy. Travel-time comparison also requires kinematics and understanding how the component of gravity along each track determines acceleration; energy conservation alone does not describe the timing of motion.

Comparing final speeds requires conservation of mechanical energy. Comparing travel times requires kinematics and Newton’s second law to analyze how track slope affects acceleration and the resulting speed throughout each descent.

This ballistic pendulum problem combines a perfectly inelastic collision with subsequent upward motion. It requires conservation of linear momentum during impact, conservation of mechanical energy during the rise, and an explanation of kinetic energy loss in the collision.

The question assesses motor efficiency by comparing useful gravitational potential energy gain with electrical energy input determined from power and time. Explaining systematic energy losses also requires work, energy, and power concepts.

Determining motor efficiency requires comparing useful gravitational potential energy gained with electrical energy input calculated from power and time. Explaining systematic losses also relies on energy transfer and dissipation.

This ballistic pendulum problem combines a perfectly inelastic collision, analyzed using conservation of linear momentum, with a subsequent rise, analyzed using conservation of mechanical energy. Explaining kinetic energy loss during embedding also requires collision and energy concepts.
The question assesses impulse as the area under a force-time graph and its relationship to change in linear momentum, final velocity, and reversal of direction. These concepts require only Unit 4.
The question assesses impulse as the area under a force-time graph and the impulse–momentum relationship, including how momentum changes determine final velocity and reversal of direction.

The question centers on rolling without slipping. Comparing arrival times and final speeds requires rotational inertia, the relationship between linear and rotational motion, and conservation of energy involving gravitational potential, translational kinetic, and rotational kinetic energy.

Locating the center of mass from support-force measurements requires translational force balance and rotational equilibrium. The procedure, relationships, and consistency check use center of mass, free-body diagrams, and torque balance.

The question centers on rolling without slipping. Comparing arrival times and final speeds requires rotational inertia, the relationship between translational and rotational motion, rotational kinetic energy, and conservation of energy for a gravitational potential-energy decrease.

Locating the center of mass from support forces requires translational force balance and rotational torque balance. The procedure and consistency check center on static equilibrium, with center-of-mass concepts from Unit 2 and torque relationships from Unit 5.

The item focuses on graphing and interpreting position, velocity, and acceleration in simple harmonic motion, including their phase relationships. Identifying maximum kinetic energy also draws on energy of simple harmonic oscillators within Unit 7.

The item centers on hydrostatic pressure as a function of depth, using the pressure-depth slope to determine liquid density. Atmospheric pressure, sensor offsets, uncertainty, and constant depth errors are analyzed within the fluid-pressure model.

The item centers on conservation of energy with nonconservative work, relating spring potential energy, frictional energy loss, and gravitational potential energy. Unit 2 is required to determine kinetic friction; Unit 3 provides work and energy principles and the quadratic dependence on spring compression.

The item tests the hydrostatic pressure–depth relationship, using its slope to determine liquid density. Data collection, atmospheric-pressure correction, uncertainty analysis, and constant depth-offset effects all center on fluid pressure.

The item centers on conservation of energy with nonconservative work, relating spring potential energy to gravitational potential energy. Calculating frictional work requires kinetic friction and the normal force from Unit 2. The compression comparison tests the quadratic dependence of spring energy.

The question primarily assesses aligned position, velocity, and acceleration graphs and their phase relationships in SHM. Identifying maximum kinetic energy also draws on the energy of simple harmonic oscillators within Unit 7.

Finding fall time and impact speed requires constant-acceleration kinematics. Explaining the constant acceleration requires understanding gravitational force and Newton’s second law under negligible air resistance.
The item focuses on kinetic friction and how its coefficient determines friction force and deceleration. It requires normal-force balance and Newton’s second law, all within Unit 2.

The item centers on energy partition and speed in mass-spring oscillations, requiring kinetic energy, spring potential energy, and conservation of energy. It also tests the amplitude independence of the period of an ideal simple harmonic oscillator.

The item primarily assesses energy in a mass-spring oscillator, including kinetic versus spring potential energy and speed from energy conservation. It also requires understanding that an ideal oscillator’s period is independent of amplitude.

Part (a) requires constant-acceleration kinematics to determine fall time and final speed. Part (b) requires gravitational force and Newton’s second law to explain constant acceleration when air resistance is neglected.

The experiment investigates average mechanical power and its dependence on climbing time. Identifying the measured variables and an appropriate control requires understanding power as gravitational potential energy gained per unit time.

The question focuses on kinetic friction and how its coefficient affects deceleration. Answering requires determining the normal and friction forces and applying Newton’s second law, all within Unit 2.

The item assesses one-dimensional constant-acceleration relationships among velocity, displacement, and time, including interpreting velocity signs and a change in direction when velocity passes through zero.

The experiment investigates average mechanical power and its dependence on climbing time. Identifying experimental variables and controls requires understanding the power relationship given in the question; no other physics unit is needed.

The item assesses one-dimensional constant-acceleration relationships among velocity, displacement, and time, including identifying a turnaround and interpreting velocity signs as directions of motion.

The item requires resolving gravitational and normal forces along perpendicular axes and applying Newton’s second law to derive acceleration and normal force, including explaining cancellation of mass.

The question requires resolving gravitational and normal forces on an incline and applying Newton’s second law to determine acceleration and normal force. Mass independence follows from the relationship between gravitational force and inertia.
Both parts require conservation of mechanical energy, relating gravitational potential energy to translational kinetic energy and explaining how the final speed depends on the starting height.
Both parts require conservation of mechanical energy, relating gravitational potential energy to translational kinetic energy and explaining how the final speed depends on the initial height.

The experiment examines how launch angle affects horizontal range in two-dimensional projectile motion. Identifying variables and explaining why launch speed must be controlled require kinematics, not analysis of the spring launcher’s forces or energy.

The experiment concerns how launch angle affects horizontal range in two-dimensional projectile motion. Identifying variables and controlling launch speed requires understanding the roles of initial velocity and angle, not spring-force or energy analysis.

The question centers on the limiting static friction between stacked blocks and the onset of slipping. Newton’s second law relates the frictional force on the top block to its acceleration and explains what happens when the required force exceeds maximum static friction.

The question centers on the maximum static friction between stacked blocks and the onset of slipping. Newton’s second law relates friction to the top block’s acceleration and explains its behavior when the applied force exceeds the no-slip threshold.

The question focuses on relative motion: determining catch-up time from initial separation and relative velocity, then explaining how changing the closing speed affects that time. Only kinematics is required.

Focuses on average versus instantaneous power and work from changes in kinetic energy. Uniform-acceleration kinematics and Newton’s second law connect the cyclist’s changing speed to the force and instantaneous power.

The question uses relative velocity to determine when one car catches another and how changing the closing speed affects catch-up time. Only constant-velocity kinematics and relative motion from Unit 1 are required.

The item focuses on Hooke’s law, spring extension under static loads, and extracting a spring constant from a graph. Force equilibrium relates the hanging masses’ weights to spring forces; experimental controls and the elastic region are integral to this spring-force investigation.

The item centers on average and instantaneous power and the work–energy relationship. Uniformly accelerated motion provides the kinematics, while Newton’s second law connects constant acceleration to constant net force for explaining how instantaneous power changes with speed.

The experiment centers on Hooke’s law, spring force, and static force balance with hanging weights. Identifying variables and interpreting a force-extension graph to determine the spring constant require Unit 2 content.

The item assesses gravitational potential energy, translational kinetic energy, and the relationship between nonconservative work and changes in mechanical energy. Friction and air resistance are treated through energy loss, without requiring force analysis.

The question uses gravitational potential energy, translational kinetic energy, and nonconservative work to analyze changes in mechanical energy. Interpreting the work’s sign requires understanding energy loss, not calculating frictional forces.

The item emphasizes constructing and interpreting a velocity-versus-time graph, using its areas to determine displacement, and explaining average velocity across distinct motion phases. All required concepts are one-dimensional kinematics.

The item emphasizes constructing and interpreting a velocity-versus-time graph, using its areas to determine displacement, and explaining average velocity across different motion phases. All required concepts concern one-dimensional kinematics.

The item centers on applying Newton’s second law to an Atwood machine, using free-body diagrams and ideal string/pulley assumptions to determine acceleration and tension and explain how changing a mass affects the net force and total inertia.

The item centers on applying Newton’s second law to coupled masses using free-body diagrams and ideal string/pulley assumptions. Calculating acceleration and tension, then explaining the effect of changing one mass, requires force and translational dynamics.

The experiment targets kinetic friction and requires relating friction to the normal force. The derivation explicitly uses the work-energy theorem and translational kinetic energy to connect initial speed with stopping distance and explain mass cancellation.

The item assesses two-dimensional projectile motion, including resolving velocity components, deriving and applying range relationships, and determining maximum height and flight time. Comparing complementary launch angles also relies on projectile-motion kinematics.

The item focuses on determining the coefficient of kinetic friction. It requires kinetic friction and normal-force relationships from Unit 2, plus work, translational kinetic energy, and the work-energy theorem from Unit 3. No kinematics equations are needed.

The item assesses two-dimensional projectile motion, including resolving velocity components, deriving and applying range relationships, and comparing complementary launch angles. All required concepts fall within kinematics; gravitational acceleration is supplied.

The conical pendulum requires force components, vertical equilibrium, and centripetal acceleration. Circular-path geometry and the relationship between speed, distance, and period also require kinematics.

The item centers on energy conservation with gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, and work done by friction. Determining friction on the second incline also requires normal force and kinetic friction concepts from Unit 2.
The conical pendulum requires resolving tension into components and applying Newton’s second law to circular motion. Kinematic relationships connect the circular path’s radius, speed, and period.

The item tests independence of horizontal and vertical projectile motion, experimental controls, and vertical constant-acceleration kinematics. Negligible air resistance is a condition of the projectile-motion model; no force analysis is required.

The question primarily applies conservation of energy, including energy dissipated by friction, to determine speed and maximum height. Unit 2 is required to calculate kinetic friction from the normal force and analyze how changing the friction coefficient affects the motion.

The item tests independence of horizontal and vertical projectile motion, experimental controls, and vertical constant-acceleration kinematics. Negligible air resistance is a standard projectile-motion assumption; no force analysis is required.
The item assesses relationships among displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time during uniformly accelerated and constant-velocity motion in one dimension.
The item requires one-dimensional kinematic relationships among acceleration, velocity, time, and displacement for uniformly accelerated and constant-velocity motion.
The item assesses interpreting a velocity-time graph to determine acceleration and displacement, and translating it into a position-time graph. All required concepts are kinematics.

The item assesses interpreting a velocity-time graph: relating its slope to acceleration, its area to displacement, and its changing velocity to the shape of a position-time graph. Only kinematics is required.

The central task applies Newton’s second law to a connected two-mass system to determine acceleration, tension, and a threshold mass. Free-body diagrams and force components require Unit 2; interpreting signed acceleration and distinguishing acceleration direction from motion require Unit 1.

Parts (a)–(c) require two-dimensional projectile kinematics, separating horizontal and vertical motion. Part (d) requires force analysis and Newton’s laws to explain constant horizontal velocity when no horizontal net force acts.

The central task is applying Newton’s second law to a connected two-mass system using free-body diagrams and force components. Kinematics is also needed to interpret the acceleration’s sign and distinguish acceleration direction from direction of motion.

Parts (a)–(c) assess two-dimensional projectile motion using independent horizontal and vertical kinematics. Part (d) requires force analysis and Newton’s first or second law to explain constant horizontal velocity when no horizontal net force acts.
The item applies Newton’s second law to determine normal force, horizontal net force, and acceleration, with kinetic friction as a contributing force. All required concepts belong to Unit 2.

The item centers on applying Newton’s second law to determine normal force, net horizontal force, and acceleration, with kinetic friction as a contributing force. All required concepts belong to Unit 2.

The item assesses circular motion through the centripetal-force requirement at the top of a vertical loop, including minimum contact speed and the magnitude and direction of the normal force. Newton’s second law and force analysis are required; energy and rotational dynamics are not.

The question requires resolving the gravitational force into vector components parallel and perpendicular to the incline, then applying Newton’s second law to determine the normal force and acceleration.

The item assesses circular motion through the centripetal acceleration requirement and Newton’s second law at the top of a loop, including the minimum-contact condition and the magnitude and direction of the normal force.

The question applies Newton’s second law to determine normal force and acceleration on an incline. Resolving gravitational force into parallel and perpendicular components also requires vector decomposition.

The item focuses on circular motion on a frictionless banked curve, requiring force components, Newton’s second law, and centripetal acceleration to identify the appropriate speed and explain behavior at higher speeds.
The item focuses on circular motion on a frictionless banked curve, using force components and Newton’s second law to relate banking angle, radius, and speed and explain motion at excessive speed.

The question centers on work done by applied and friction forces, net work, and the work-energy theorem relating kinetic energy to speed. All forces are supplied, so force dynamics and friction models are not required.

The item focuses on work done by applied and frictional forces, net work, and the work-energy theorem. Initial and final kinetic energy connect the net work to final speed. All required concepts are in Unit 3; friction is already specified.

The item centers on conservation of mechanical energy as elastic potential energy becomes translational kinetic energy and then gravitational potential energy. All parts require only Unit 3 energy concepts.

The central topic is mechanical power and efficiency. Determining the lifting force also requires Newton’s laws: constant velocity implies zero net force, so the motor’s force balances the elevator’s weight.

The item centers on conservation of mechanical energy as elastic potential energy becomes translational kinetic energy and then gravitational potential energy. All parts require only Unit 3 concepts, including potential energy, kinetic energy, and energy conservation.

Power and efficiency are the central concepts. Constant velocity implies zero acceleration (Unit 1); Newton’s laws establish the lifting force (Unit 2); mechanical power and efficiency determine output and input power (Unit 3).

The item emphasizes the period and frequency of spring–mass SHM, including half-cycle timing and amplitude independence. It also requires mechanical energy, elastic potential energy, and kinetic energy to analyze maximum speed and amplitude dependence.

The main focus is the period and frequency of spring-block SHM, including half-period timing and amplitude independence. Calculating mechanical energy and maximum speed also requires spring potential energy, kinetic energy, and conservation of energy.
